Determine which quadrant contains a given point
Recognize the sign patterns for coordinates in each quadrant
Use coordinates to describe the location of points on a plane

CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.6.G.A.3 - Draw polygons in the coordinate plane

pedagogical.assessment: Students predict the outcome for each panel before sending, then explain the structural reason the fixed panel contains the attack.
misconceptionsAddressed: Believing input validation/blocklists are the fix, rather than separating data from code.

Acid rain is caused by a single pollutant (both SO2 and NOx contribute)
Acid rain only affects lakes (it also damages forests, soils, and buildings)

Ask students to predict which impacts would recover first if emissions were reduced
Challenge students to explain why transboundary pollution requires international cooperation

title: Biomagnification Through a Food Web
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Ecology
description: Interactive trophic pyramid showing how pollutant concentrations magnify approximately 10x at each level with adjustable initial concentration

learningObjectives: Compare pollutant concentrations across trophic levels and explain why top predators are most affected
Calculate the approximate magnification factor between adjacent trophic levels
Predict when toxin concentrations will exceed danger thresholds
Connect biomagnification to real-world examples like DDT and mercury
prerequisites: Understanding of food webs and trophic levels
Knowledge of producer, consumer, and predator concepts
Familiarity with parts per million (ppm) as a concentration unit

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Slider-driven quantitative exploration with visual danger indicators
keyQuestions: Why are top predators most vulnerable to persistent pollutants?
What initial water concentration is truly 'safe' for the entire food web?
How does the 10x magnification factor explain why DDT nearly drove eagles to extinction?
Why do fish consumption advisories target large predatory fish like tuna and swordfish?
commonMisconceptions: If the water concentration is safe for humans, the food web is safe (biomagnification can create dangerous levels at higher trophic levels)
All pollutants biomagnify equally (only persistent, fat-soluble chemicals accumulate significantly)
Biomagnification only happens in aquatic ecosystems (it also occurs in terrestrial food webs)
assessmentOpportunities: Have students calculate concentrations at each trophic level for a given initial value
Ask students to determine the maximum safe initial concentration for top predators
Challenge students to explain why banning DDT helped eagle populations recover using the magnification model

creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Ecology
description: Interactive network graph showing material and energy flow connections between 13 terrestrial and aquatic biomes with disruption simulation

learningObjectives: Assess how material and energy flows connect different biomes across the planet
Identify types of connections between biomes including migration, water flow, nutrient transport, and atmospheric connections
Predict cascading effects when one biome is disrupted
Evaluate which biomes are most critical to global ecological stability
prerequisites: Knowledge of major terrestrial and aquatic biome types

Basic familiarity with migration and nutrient cycling

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Network visualization with disruption simulation for systems thinking
keyQuestions: Which biome has the most connections to other biomes?
What happens to distant biomes when a tropical rainforest is disrupted?
How do atmospheric connections differ from direct material flows?
Why must conservation efforts consider biome connectivity rather than protecting individual biomes in isolation?
commonMisconceptions: Biomes are independent and isolated from each other (they are connected by multiple material and energy flows)
Only adjacent biomes affect each other (bird migration and atmospheric transport connect distant biomes)
Aquatic and terrestrial biomes are separate systems (they are connected through water cycles, nutrient runoff, and migration)
assessmentOpportunities: Have students rank biomes by connectivity and predict which disruption would cause the most cascading damage
Ask students to trace a specific material flow (e.g., nutrients from forests to oceans) through multiple connected biomes
Challenge students to design a global conservation strategy that prioritizes the most connected biomes

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Calculator-based quantitative exploration with disturbance scenarios
keyQuestions: Can a healthy forest ever become a carbon source? Under what conditions?
Which ecosystem type has the largest carbon sink capacity and why?
How do fire, drought, and warming each affect the carbon budget differently?

commonMisconceptions: Forests always absorb CO2 (disturbed or old-growth forests can be carbon neutral or even sources)
NPP and NEP are the same thing (NEP also accounts for heterotrophic respiration by decomposers and animals)
Warming only affects photosynthesis (it actually increases respiration rates more than photosynthesis, potentially flipping sink to source)
assessmentOpportunities: Have students calculate NPP and NEP from given GPP, Ra, and Rh values
Ask students to determine the tipping point where a tropical forest switches from sink to source under warming
Challenge students to rank the five ecosystems by carbon sink capacity and explain the ecological reasons for differences

What happens to biodiversity during succession, and why?
How do disturbances reset or alter the succession process?

title: Thermal Inversion Simulator
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Ecology
description: Split-screen particle simulation comparing normal atmospheric conditions with thermal inversion, showing how pollutants accumulate when trapped by a warm air layer

learningObjectives: Explain how thermal inversions trap pollutants near the ground by comparing normal and inverted temperature profiles
Analyze the relationship between emission rates, atmospheric conditions, and air quality
Connect thermal inversion events to real-world smog and public health impacts
prerequisites: Basic understanding of air pollution sources
Familiarity with temperature and altitude relationships

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Animated particle simulation with side-by-side comparison
keyQuestions: How does the temperature profile of the atmosphere affect pollutant dispersal?
Why does a thermal inversion act as a 'lid' trapping pollution near the ground?
What geographic features make some cities more vulnerable to inversions?
How do weather forecasts help cities prepare for poor air quality events?

How might one tipping point cascade into triggering others?

Students may believe all climate changes are reversible if we reduce emissions, not understanding hysteresis

A checkbox draws the suspect's claimed 'Home all day' ring; whenever the highlighted photo's GPS is not Home, a red banner and panel status flag the alibi as contradicted, naming the place and time. pedagogical.interactionPattern: Two stacked charts fill the left of the canvas. The top gas chromatogram plots detector abundance versus retention time and shows the unknown as one dominant filled peak; the bottom mass spectrum plots relative intensity versus m/z as labeled bars for the unknown's fragmentation pattern. A dropdown selects one of four reference candidates (Caffeine, Aspirin, Pseudoephedrine, Compound X). 'Overlay & Score' draws the candidate's retention peak and spectrum in a second color over the unknown and reports a retention-time match, a fragment-pattern match, and an overall percentage in a verdict panel. 'New Unknown' deterministically cycles which substance is the unknown; 'Reveal Match' discloses the unknown's true identity.
pedagogical.assessment: Application with immediate feedback: only when the student selects the candidate whose retention time AND fragmentation pattern both match the unknown does the overall score reach the CONFIRMED band. Mismatched candidates score low even if they share an occasional fragment, making the presumptive-versus-confirmatory distinction concrete.
pedagogical.modelType: Qualitative analytical model: each library substance has a stored retention time and a set of m/z fragment peaks. The retention-time score falls off with the time difference; the spectral score is the intensity-weighted fraction of the unknown's fragments the candidate reproduces within an m/z tolerance; the overall score is a weighted blend that reaches 100% only for the true substance.

title: Live Hash & Tamper Detector
description: Compute and compare cryptographic hashes of digital evidence, entirely in the browser and offline. Type evidence text and the tool computes its MD5 (128-bit) and SHA-256 (256-bit) hex digests live. A 'Tamper: flip one character' button mutates a single character and re-hashes, highlighting every changed hex digit and counting them so the avalanche effect is visible at a glance. The avalanche count is the Hamming distance in hex digits between the pre-edit and post-edit digests; the compare verdict is exact string equality of two SHA-256 digests.

A dropdown selects one of five samples. 'Run Presumptive Test' animates the reagent drop and develops the color; a right-hand verdict panel explains that a pink flash is presumptive only. 'Run Confirmatory Test' (enabled after screening) resolves the ground truth — only Stain A and the blood simulant are truly blood, while horseradish is revealed as a false positive. 'Reset' returns to the sample-ready state.
pedagogical.assessment: Evaluation with staged feedback: the student screens each sample, reads the presumptive verdict, then commits to a confirmatory test that either validates or overturns the screen. Meeting the horseradish false positive forces the student to articulate why a presumptive positive means 'consistent with blood, confirm it' rather than 'this is blood.'
pedagogical.modelType: Qualitative peroxidase model: each sample carries a presumptive reaction strength (0 to 1) that drives a color lerp from the sample color toward pink, plus an independent confirmatory truth flag for whether the stain is actually blood. Blood simulant and Stain A are true positives, horseradish is a strong false positive, rust reacts weakly, and ketchup is negative.

Score striation correlation and interpret a match versus no-match verdict.
Exclude a tool on class characteristics and identify the source tool on individual characteristics.
educational.prerequisites: Familiarity with toolmarks, striations, and the difference between class and individual characteristics

pedagogical.interactionPattern: The crime-scene toolmark is drawn as a strip of vertical striation lines at the top; the selected suspect tool's test mark is a second strip below it, separated by a comparison-microscope bridge line. A dropdown chooses among three suspect tools; a slider shifts the suspect strip horizontally to align its striations with the scene mark. 'Score Alignment' computes the percentage of scene striations that coincide with a suspect striation within tolerance at the current shift, prints a MATCH or NO MATCH verdict, and draws green vertical guides through the coinciding lines. 'Reset' returns the shift to zero. A class-width readout marks a tool as excluded on class when its width differs from the scene mark.
pedagogical.assessment: Analysis with immediate feedback: the student first checks the class width to see whether a tool can be excluded outright, then slides the striations into alignment and scores the individual match. Because only one tool's striation pattern truly aligns, a wrong tool never reaches the match threshold no matter how it is shifted, reinforcing that a real identification survives small alignment adjustments while a coincidental one does not.
pedagogical.modelType: Translation-correlation model: each strip is a set of striation positions given as fractions of strip width. The suspect strip has a fixed offset plus a user shift; two striations coincide when their pixel positions fall within a fixed tolerance. The correlation score is the fraction of scene striations with a coinciding suspect striation. Only the matching tool shares the scene's positions, so it reaches 100% at the aligning shift.
controls: 'Tool' dropdown — choose Tool 1 (Screwdriver), Tool 2 (Chisel), or Tool 3 (Bolt cutter)
'Shift (align)' slider — translate the suspect strip horizontally to align striations
'Score Alignment' button — compute the correlation percentage and show the verdict
'Reset' button — return the shift to zero and clear the verdict

pedagogical.interactionPattern: A TLC plate occupies the left ~40% of the canvas with four lanes (Questioned, Reference 1, 2, 3); the right ~60% is a result-interpretation panel. A dashed origin line and a blue solvent-front line bracket the plate. 'Run Chromatography' animates the solvent front rising from the origin while each dye spot migrates to its Rf-proportional height. 'Toggle UV' switches the plate to a dark fluorescence view that reveals UV-only components (e.g., an optical brightener). 'Calculate Rf' overlays Rf values next to each spot and in the table. Two dropdowns select the questioned ink type and the reference lane set. The panel shows the questioned ink's per-component spot distance and Rf, a component-by-component match count against each reference with green-check / red-X indicators, and a Match Determination box.
pedagogical.assessment: Interpretation and explanation: students run the separation, read the Rf values they compute, and use the component-by-component comparison to decide which reference the questioned ink matches. The Match Determination box confirms or contradicts their reading, and switching to UV tests whether they account for hidden fluorescent components.
pedagogical.modelType: Chromatography model: each ink is a list of dye components, each with a color, a characteristic Rf, and an optional UV-only flag. Spot position is computed as origin minus Rf times the current solvent-front travel; matching compares questioned components to reference components within an Rf tolerance and a color-distance tolerance.
controls: 'Questioned ink' dropdown — ballpoint, rollerball, gel pen, fountain pen
'Reference set' dropdown — choose which inks fill the three reference lanes

'Toggle UV' button — switch between white-light and UV fluorescence views
'Calculate Rf' button — show/hide Rf value overlays

title: Triangulation Measurement Technique
description: Apply triangulation to record evidence position on a scaled crime-scene sketch. Drag an evidence item around an overhead room floor plan and read the live straight-line distances from two fixed reference corners (A and B), computed with the Pythagorean theorem. Adjust the room dimensions with sliders, and record each measurement to a log the way an investigator fills in a sketch sheet.

subject: Forensic Science
Crime Scene Investigation
Evidence Collection
Crime Scene Sketching
Measurement

educational.topic: Recording the position of evidence with the triangulation method on a scaled crime-scene sketch
learningObjectives: Apply the triangulation method: measure an evidence item's straight-line distance from two fixed reference points.
Use the Pythagorean theorem to relate an item's (x, y) coordinates to its distances from two corners.
Read distances in centimeters from a scaled overhead floor plan.
Record multiple evidence items to a measurement log as on a real sketch sheet.
educational.prerequisites: Familiarity with the Pythagorean theorem and the idea of measuring from fixed reference points

pedagogical.interactionPattern: An overhead floor plan of a room fills the left ~72% of the canvas, with a 1-meter grid and two fixed green reference corners (A at upper-left, B at upper-right). A draggable orange evidence dot is connected to A and B by blue dashed lines whose midpoints show the live distance in centimeters; the dot also displays its (x, y) coordinates measured from A. The right panel shows the live distances and coordinates plus a measurement log. Two sliders set the room width and length (3-10 m). 'Record Measurement' appends the current item number and its A/B distances to the log; 'Clear Log' empties it.
pedagogical.assessment: Application with immediate feedback: the student drags the item and the distances recompute via the Pythagorean theorem, confirming whether they understand what triangulation measures. Recording several items builds a log that mirrors how positions are documented on a scaled sketch, and changing the room size tests whether the student understands that distances are measured to fixed corners.
pedagogical.modelType: Geometric model: the evidence item has a position in meters from corner A; distance to A is sqrt(x^2 + y^2) and distance to B is sqrt((W - x)^2 + y^2), where W is the room width. Pixel geometry is scaled to keep the room's real aspect ratio as the sliders change its dimensions.
controls: Draggable evidence item (orange dot) anywhere within the room
'Record Measurement' button — append the current distances to the log
'Clear Log' button — empty the measurement log

learningObjectives: Understand how simple iterative rules can create complex patterns

prerequisites: Basic understanding of line segments and geometric transformations

controls.name: recursionSlider
controls.label: Recursion Level
controls.purpose: Controls the number of iterations in the Koch curve construction. Level 0 shows a straight line, while higher levels show increasingly complex fractal patterns.

variables: baselineY: Vertical position of the fractal baseline
canvasWidth: Responsive width of the drawing canvas
model.algorithm: Recursive Koch curve generation using geometric transformation
model.description: At each recursion level, every line segment is divided into three equal parts, and the middle third is replaced with two sides of an equilateral triangle. This process creates a self-similar fractal pattern.
equations: Length at level n: (4/3)^n × original length
Number of segments at level n: 4^n
assumptions: The fractal is displayed as a 2D projection
Maximum recursion level is limited to 6 for performance
Discrete rendering approximates the theoretical continuous curve
limitations: Does not show the full Koch snowflake (three curves arranged in a triangle)
Does not animate the iterative construction process
Performance may decrease at high recursion levels on slower devices

assessmentOpportunities: Pattern recognition at different recursion levels
Mathematical calculation of length and segments
Understanding of fractal dimension concept
Connection to real-world fractal examples
commonMisconceptions: Believing the curve will eventually smooth out
Thinking infinite length means infinite area
Confusion between recursion level and fractal dimension

dublin_core.description: An interactive visualization of the Sierpinski triangle fractal demonstrating recursive subdivision and self-similar patterns. Students can adjust the recursion depth from 0 to 7 levels to explore how simple rules create complex fractal patterns.

learning_objectives: Understand the concept of recursive subdivision in geometry

prerequisites: Basic understanding of triangles and geometric shapes

parameters.purpose: Determines how many levels of recursion to apply when drawing the fractal

displays.label: Triangles
displays.description: Shows total number of triangles drawn (3^depth)

key_variables: recursionDepth - Number of recursive subdivisions to perform
vertices - Coordinates of triangle vertices for each recursion level
algorithm: - Create 4 smaller triangles from these midpoints
- Draw only the 3 outer triangles (skip center)
- Recursively apply to each of the 3 triangles
equations: Triangle count = 3^n where n is recursion depth
Total area approaches 0 as n approaches infinity
assumptions: Perfect geometric precision in subdivision
Equilateral starting triangle
Infinite recursion not practically achievable (limited to depth 7)
limitations: Performance degrades beyond depth 7 due to exponential triangle count
Does not show the mathematical properties of infinite recursion
Visual resolution limits ability to see very small triangles at high depths

learningObjective: Given a real-world organizational task, students can identify which entity in the scenario plays each of the six component roles (Hardware, Software, Network, Data, User, Business Process).
audience: Undergraduate students (sophomore/junior) in an introductory Information Systems course.
prerequisites: None beyond the chapter narrative introducing the six components.

educational.audience: Undergraduate sophomores and juniors taking an introductory Information Systems course (CIS, MIS, or general-studies IS).
educational.duration: 5-10 minutes of in-class exploration plus a short writing exercise.
educational.prerequisites: Reading of Chapter 1 sections on the six components of an information system.
educational.learningObjective: Given a real-world organizational task, students can identify which entity in the scenario plays each of the six component roles.
educational.assessment: Students write one paragraph mapping each of the six roles to an organizational task drawn from their own life (e.g., ordering food delivery, returning a library book).

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Click-to-reveal node exploration paired with a scenario toggle. The same six components remain on screen across scenarios; only the right-panel definitions, examples, and what-breaks-if-missing answers change.
pedagogical.designRationale: Apply-level objectives demand transfer of an abstract model to concrete situations. Cycling the same six nodes through three scenarios forces students to recognize structural sameness underneath surface variation — the core Apply move.
pedagogical.systemsThinkingNotes: The complete graph (K6) is itself a teaching device: every component is connected to every other component because in a working IS, every component depends on every other one. The 'what breaks if missing' framing surfaces second-order effects and discourages the rookie mistake of treating any one component in isolation.

key_principles: Working memory has limited capacity (typically 4-7 chunks)
Long-term memory has virtually unlimited capacity
Learning requires transferring information from working to long-term memory
Cognitive load is additive across all three types
Effective design manages all three types of load
research_support: Meta-analyses show effect sizes of 0.4-1.0 for load reduction
Split-attention effect consistently demonstrates extraneous load impact
Worked example effect shows intrinsic load management
Expertise reversal effect demonstrates load relativity

common_misconceptions: More information is always better (ignores capacity limits)
Attractive design is more important than clear design (adds extraneous load)
All cognitive effort is productive (ignores extraneous load)
Content difficulty can't be managed (ignores chunking strategies)

assessmentOpportunities: Quiz mode tests students' ability to match scenarios to the correct epistemic region
Ask students to create their own examples for each region

How does the category bucket relate to xAPI profiles like CMI5?
When should you reach for the other bucket vs. a custom extension?
commonMisconceptions: Treating Parent and Grouping as interchangeable.
Forgetting that category is required by some profiles (CMI5).
Using the other bucket for data that should be a typed extension.
